turns.prompt: Can you explain how a bicycle stays upright when it's moving? I've never really understood it.
turns.response:
A moving bicycle stays upright mainly because it can steer its wheels back underneath you when you start to tip.

Imagine balancing a broom upright on your palm. If it leans left, you move your hand left to get back under it. A bicycle does something similar: if it starts leaning left, steering left helps bring its wheels back under your weight.

While riding, you make these small steering corrections almost without noticing. The bike’s geometry also helps: on many bicycles, a lean naturally encourages the front wheel to turn toward that lean. That’s one reason a bike can sometimes roll upright for a while even without a rider.

Moving makes this possible because steering changes where the wheels go. At a standstill, simply turning the handlebars does very little to move your support underneath you—so balancing is much harder.

You might have heard that the spinning wheels keep it upright “like a gyroscope.” They do contribute to how a bicycle behaves, but they aren’t the whole explanation, and gyroscopic effects aren’t necessary for a bike to balance.

The useful picture is this: riding a bike isn’t holding it perfectly upright—it’s continually catching tiny falls by steering.

turns.prompt: So is it mostly the gyroscopic effect, or something else?
turns.response:
Mostly something else: steering corrections that keep the wheels underneath your center of mass.

If you tip left, steering left makes the bike follow a curved path and helps arrest the fall. You make these corrections instinctively, and the bike’s geometry can help it steer into a lean on its own.

The wheels’ gyroscopic effect influences that response, but it isn’t the main thing holding you up. Think “balancing a broom by moving your hand underneath it,” not “a spinning top resisting a tilt.”

turns.prompt: Why is it so much harder to balance when you go very slowly?
turns.response:
Because at low speed, steering has much less ability to correct a lean.

At a normal riding speed, a tiny turn of the handlebars quickly redirects the wheels underneath you. At a crawl, that same steering movement barely changes their path before you’ve tipped farther. You need bigger, more carefully timed corrections, and it’s easier to run out of room to recover.

Think of balancing a broom on your palm—but now your hand is only allowed to move very slowly. You can still catch a small lean, but a larger one quickly gets away from you.

The wheels also have less gyroscopic effect at low speed, but the main difficulty is losing that steering-based ability to catch yourself.
